readings.title: The Mail-Coach Passengers
readings.author: Hans Christian Andersen; adapted by Frances Jenkins Olcott
readings.challenge: Guess who each passenger is before the story gives the name.
readings.focus: At midnight on New Year’s Eve twelve strangers step out of a coach, and each one’s clothes, luggage and talk show which month of the year it is.
readings.context: Frances Jenkins Olcott gathered stories for every holiday in Good Stories for Great Holidays (1914), shortening or retelling many of them. Hans Christian Andersen, the Danish storyteller, wrote this tale, which other books call “Twelve by the Mail.” A mail-coach is a big carriage that carried letters and passengers; a sentry guards the town gate; a passport is a paper that says who you are; a profession is a person’s work. Carnival is a time of parties just before Lent, the weeks of fasting before Easter; a bung is the stopper of a barrel; a weather prophet foretells the weather; an April fool is someone tricked on the first of April; the harvest home is a feast at the end of harvest; a parish is a village and its church. It is read on New Year’s Day, when the twelve months arrive again.

excerpt.locator: New Year’s Day, “The Mail-Coach Passengers,” the whole story without its byline; opens “It was bitterly cold. The sky glittered with stars, and not a breeze stirred. “Bump,”--an…”; closes “…do not know, and probably even they do not know themselves, for we live in strange times.”.

questions.prompt: Who is the first passenger, and what clues tell you, even before he gives his name?
facilitatorNotes: January. He wears bearskin and fur boots, his ships are frozen in, he gives thirty-one balls, one for each day, and he brings his accounts, as people do when a year begins.
evidence: arrayed in bearskin and fur boots
_My name is January_.

questions.prompt: Why does the second passenger say he has not long to live? What does he mean by “Sometimes they pop me in a day extra”?
facilitatorNotes: He is February, the shortest month, with twenty-eight days; in a leap year he gets a twenty-ninth. Children can check on a calendar.
evidence: only twenty-eight days
Sometimes they pop me in a day extra

questions.prompt: Pick a passenger from spring or summer. How do the clothes, luggage or words fit that month?
facilitatorNotes: For example, April brings a summer wardrobe but says it would be foolish to wear it yet, because April weather keeps changing; May wears a summer dress with overshoes; July carries almost nothing in the heat. Accept any passenger tied to a detail in the story.
evidence: sometimes I'm obliged to be in a good humor, and sometimes a bad one
He had very little luggage because it was so cumbersome in the great heat.

questions.prompt: The Captain will keep each passport for a month and then write down how that stranger behaved. Why can nobody say yet what the twelve have brought? What would you like the new year to bring?
facilitatorNotes: The year has not happened yet; each month’s gifts are known only when it has passed, and the story says even the months may not know. Children can name one hope for the coming year.
evidence: When that has passed, I shall write the behavior of each stranger on his passport.
probably even they do not know themselves

readings.title: The Loveliest Rose in the World
readings.author: Hans Christian Andersen; adapted by Frances Jenkins Olcott
readings.workTitle: The Loveliest Rose in the World
readings.challenge: Keep count of the roses people name, and decide why the wise man turns each one down.
readings.focus: To save a dying queen, people name the loveliest rose in the world, each a different kind of love, until her son reads to her of Christ’s death on the cross.
readings.context: Frances Jenkins Olcott gathered stories for every holiday in Good Stories for Great Holidays (1914), shortening or retelling many of them. Hans Christian Andersen wrote this tale. In it a rose stands for a kind of love, so “the loveliest rose” means the greatest love. A symbol is a thing that stands for something else; ere means before; science is the study of how the world works; the Lord’s Table is the altar in a church; the Book is the Bible. It is read at Easter, when Christians remember Jesus’s death on the cross and celebrate his rising to life.
readings.contentNote: A queen lies dying, and the wise man speaks of a hero’s blood and of the blood of Christ on the cross.

excerpt.locator: Resurrection Day (Easter), “The Loveliest Rose in the World,” the whole story without its byline; opens “Once there reigned a queen, in whose garden were found the most glorious flowers at all…”; closes ““I see it!” she said, “he who beholds this, the loveliest rose on earth, shall never die.””.

questions.prompt: What can save the queen, according to the wise man?
facilitatorNotes: The loveliest rose in the world, the sign of the purest, brightest love, held before her eyes before they close.
evidence: Bring her the loveliest rose in the world, the rose that is the symbol of the purest, the brightest love.

questions.prompt: List the “roses” people name. What kind of love is each one?
facilitatorNotes: Young lovers; the hero who dies for his country; science, which takes a person’s sleepless nights; a mother’s joy in her waking child; the queen’s own grief over her sick child; a girl’s love of God at the altar. Each is a real kind of love.
evidence: It springs in the blooming cheeks of my sweet child
the white rose of a mother's grief

questions.prompt: The wise man says each rose is lovely, but not the one they seek. Why might the story let so many people be almost right?
facilitatorNotes: Each step builds toward the last answer and makes it stand out, while honouring every kind of love on the way. Some children will think the mother’s answer should have been enough; the wise man himself calls it lovely.
evidence: Lovely is this rose, but there is a lovelier still
not one of you has yet named the loveliest rose in the world

questions.prompt: Who finally finds the rose, and where? Why might the story give that discovery to a child?
facilitatorNotes: The queen’s little son, reading from the Bible about Jesus dying on the cross to save people; the queen sees the rose bloom from its pages. A child reading simply finds what the wise grown-ups could not. Children of any faith can say what the story believes the greatest love is: giving your life for others.
evidence: Then there came into the room a child, the queen's little son.
Greater love there is not.

readings.title: The King of the Cats
readings.author: Ernest Rhys
readings.challenge: Watch the cat while Fergus tells his story.
readings.focus: A young man lost in a mountain fog sees a funeral of cats inside a hollow oak, and when he tells of it at home, the old woman’s black cat gives itself away.
readings.context: Frances Jenkins Olcott gathered stories for every holiday in Good Stories for Great Holidays (1914), shortening or retelling many of them. This old British folk-tale is told here by Ernest Rhys. Peat is dried earth that burns like wood; the hearth is the floor of the fireplace; a funeral is the service when someone who has died is buried, and a coffin is the box they lie in; a crown and a scepter are signs of a king; cannily means cleverly; “My stars!” is an old way of saying “My goodness!” It is read on Halloween, a night for spooky stories by the fire.

excerpt.locator: Halloween, “The King of the Cats,” the whole story without its subtitle and byline; opens “Once upon a time there were two brothers who lived in a lonely house in a very lonely…”; closes “…dead, and I'm the King o' the Cats!”--Then rushed up the chimney, and was seen no more.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Fergus so late coming home?
facilitatorNotes: A mountain fog came down and he lost his way; then he followed a light to a hollow oak tree and saw something strange inside.
evidence: A mountain fog came on just as I was about to turn homewards

questions.prompt: What does Fergus see inside the hollow tree?
facilitatorNotes: What looks like a church with a funeral going on: singing, a coffin surrounded by torches, and both carried by cats, with a crown and a scepter marked on the coffin.
evidence: I seemed to be looking down into a church, where a funeral was taking place.
upon the coffin were marked a crown and a scepter

questions.prompt: Look at what the cat does while Fergus talks. Which clues tell you something is coming?
facilitatorNotes: At first she sits with half-shut eyes; then she sits up and listens as carefully as Elshender, and both brothers turn to look at her. The storyteller makes us watch the cat before anything happens.
evidence: the cat was sitting up, and seemed to be listening just as carefully and cannily as Elshender himself
Both brothers, indeed, turned their eyes on the cat

questions.prompt: What does the cat’s shout tell you about her and about the funeral? Why does the story stop right there?
facilitatorNotes: The dead king was old Peter, and she is the next King o’ the Cats, so the cats’ kingdom is real and she belongs to it. The story ends with a jump and leaves the rest to us, as a good spooky story does. Some children will wonder whether she was ever an ordinary cat; nobody can know.
evidence: old Peter's dead, and I'm the King o' the Cats!
was seen no more

readings.title: The First Harvest-Home in Plymouth
readings.author: W. De Loss Love, Jr.; adapted by Frances Jenkins Olcott
readings.challenge: Find out why the Pilgrims had so much to be thankful for that autumn.
readings.focus: After a hungry first winter at Plymouth, the Pilgrims bring in a good harvest in 1621 and share a week of feasting with Massasoit and ninety of his men.
readings.context: Frances Jenkins Olcott gathered stories for every holiday in Good Stories for Great Holidays (1914), shortening or retelling many of them. The Pilgrims were English people who lived for a time in Leyden, in Holland, and then sailed to Plymouth, in what is now Massachusetts, in 1620. The Indians in this story were the Wampanoag people, who had lived there for thousands of years; Massasoit was their leader, and a Patuxet man named Tisquantum, or Squanto, had shown the colonists how to plant corn, which this story leaves out. The Pilgrims’ governor, William Bradford, wrote in old spelling, where “yt” means that and “ye” means the. Bounteous means generous; game is wild animals hunted for food; venison is deer meat; the board is the table; exiles are people far from home. It is read on Thanksgiving, which remembers this feast.
readings.contentNote: Like many writers of his time, the author calls Massasoit a “king” and his men “braves,” and tells the story only from the Pilgrims’ side. The many deaths of the first winter are mentioned.

excerpt.locator: Thanksgiving Day, “The First Harvest-Home in Plymouth,” the whole story without its byline; opens “After prayer and fasting and a farewell feast, the Pilgrim Fathers left the City of…”; closes “…on God's gifts in Nature. It was the promise of autumnal Thanksgivings to come.”.

questions.prompt: Why did the Pilgrims watch their crops “with anxiety” in the spring of 1621?
facilitatorNotes: Their first winter had been so hard that many died of hunger and illness, and they knew their lives depended on a full harvest.
evidence: The first winter in the New World was marked by great suffering and want.
their lives depended upon a full harvest

questions.prompt: Who came to the feast, and what did they bring?
facilitatorNotes: Massasoit, the Wampanoag leader, with ninety men. They went into the woods, killed deer and gave the venison to the governor and others.
evidence: Many Indians visited the colony
killed fine deer, which they brought to the colony

questions.prompt: Find three foods from the feast. Which surprise you?
facilitatorNotes: Oysters, fish, wild turkey, maize, barley bread, geese, ducks, venison, wild grapes, and the vegetables in the verse. Some children will notice that the verse sounds like an English garden, while much of the feast came from the woods and the sea.
evidence: Oysters, fish and wild turkey, Indian maize and barley bread

questions.prompt: The story calls it a feast “worthy of their Indian guests,” but it is told only from the Pilgrims’ side. What might Massasoit’s people have said about those three days?
facilitatorNotes: Perhaps that they came as allies, brought much of the meat, and were sharing land that had long been theirs; the story never gives their words. A good answer notices whose voice is missing. Children may also enjoy the picture of everyone making merry together, which the story does show.
evidence: a feast worthy of their Indian guests
So all made merry together.
